column1: # Чем получено: implementations of HierarchicalRuleOptionsInterface and
#   Serena (primary witness), both calls with default arguments:
#   HierarchicalRuleOptionsInterface: Serena 5, grep 5. Identical sets. No discrepancy.
#   The file-MENTION grep (grep -rln) returns 20 files and is the one that is wrong: the
#   extra 10 are the interface itself, HierarchicalRuleOptionsInterface (return type), the
#   5 hierarchical wrappers (they RETURN a LevelOptionsInterface from forLevel(), they do
#   not implement it), and AbstractRule / RuleOptionKeyRecognition /
#   BaselineConfiguredThresholds (consumers). Measured, not assumed: an earlier draft of
#   this file predicted the narrow grep would find 0 (guessing the implements lists were
#   line-wrapped); running it showed all 10 are single-line
#   `final readonly class X implements LevelOptionsInterface, ThresholdAwareOptionsInterface`.
#   The implementation set below is Serena's; the narrow grep confirms it independently.
#   - An implementation reached through an abstract base class or a trait: Serena resolves
#     it, the greps do not. None exists here (all 15 classes are `final readonly class`),
#     so the two witnesses agreeing is weak evidence, not proof of the method.
#   - Anonymous classes implementing either interface (Serena would list them; none found).
#   - The "flat branch" column is decided by reading each fromArray() body by eye. A branch
#     that keys off something other than a literal `threshold`/`max_warning`/`max_error`
#   - A level class does not carry a flat branch of its own; its `threshold` shorthand is
#     handled one level down, inside ThresholdParser::parse()
#     therefore listed once rather than per class.
# TOTALS: HierarchicalRuleOptionsInterface 5 | LevelOptionsInterface 10 | with flat branch 5/5
